pages.title: Insulation resistance: IR, DAR and PI
pages.for: Is the insulation dry and clean at low stress? Put a steady d.c. voltage between core and screen, and read it over 10 minutes.
pages.rule:
PI = R10min ÷ R1min
DAR = R60s ÷ R30s
Discharge: at least 5 × the time the voltage was on
Discharge order: display shows discharged, discharge stick, hook stick, hand earth, then earths on core and screen at both ends.
Q = C × V
E = ½ × C × V²

PI: below 1 poor, 1–2 questionable, 2–4 okay, above 4 good.
DAR: below 1.25 inadequate, 1.25–1.6 satisfactory, above 1.6 excellent.
Makers' bands differ: the client's spec decides.
Red to screen, black to core.
Near 1 is the bad end: the curve is flat.
One reading roughly halves for every 10 °C rise. A ratio barely moves.

traps.text: Passing a core on one reading that beats the client's figure. A flat curve behind it points to moisture.
traps.cite: Notes p.4; Megger, Electrical insulation testing: a low PI can indicate moisture (research)

traps.text: Working the ratio upside down. PI is the 10-minute reading over the 1-minute one.
traps.cite: Notes p.4; Megger, A Stitch in Time (research)

traps.text: Lifting the earths too soon. Charge in the insulation can bring the voltage back.
traps.cite: Notes p.3; Megger, guide to testing above 1 kV (research)

traps.cite: Megger, Can we beat the heat? (research)

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: One core reads 2.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 6.0 GΩ at 10 minutes. What is its PI, and how does it rate?
pages.alt: PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 6.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.00. That sits in the 2 to 4 band, okay. 0.33 is the ratio upside down, and 4.0 is how far the reading rose.
pages.html:
PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 6.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.00. That sits in the 2 to 4 band, okay.

0.33 is the ratio upside down, and 4.0 is how far the reading rose.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: The IR test puts a steady d.c. voltage between a core and its screen. It is the same test you do on an installation, read over 10 minutes instead of once. The tester measures the tiny current that gets through the XLPE and shows it as a resistance. It answers one question: is the insulation dry and clean, at low stress? It runs after core resistance and before the sheath test. On String B it runs at 5 kV d.c.. That is the client's choice, and a practice value here.
pages.alt: core XLPE nanoamps screen IR tester 5 kV d.c. black lead, − red lead, + If it is skipped Damp or dirty insulation goes on to the high-voltage tests unseen. So does a core that passes on one reading but leaks steadily.
pages.html:
If it is skipped

Damp or dirty insulation goes on to the high-voltage tests unseen. So does a core that passes on one reading but leaks steadily.

pages.name: The why: three currents
pages.text: The current the tester sees has three parts. A charging current fills the cable's capacitance and dies away in seconds. An absorption current flows while the insulation slowly polarises. Charge inside the plastic shifts into line with the field, and that slow shift is a current. It dies away over minutes. A leakage current runs through the insulation and stays. The tester shows voltage ÷ current. So as the first two die away, the reading climbs. Water or dirt adds leakage, and leakage does not die away. It swamps the absorption, so the reading hardly climbs. The dry core climbs from 18.1 GΩ at 30 s to 64.0 GΩ at 10 minutes, a PI of 2.66. In the wet core, a steady 2083 nA of leakage swamps the absorption. It reads 2.19, 2.26 and 2.40 GΩ, a PI of 1.06. Both clear 1 GΩ at 1 minute. Against the client's 1 GΩ alone, only the climb tells them apart.
pages.alt: The current the tester sees has three parts. A charging current fills the cable's capacitance and dies away in seconds. An absorption current flows while the insulation slowly polarises. Charge inside the plastic shifts into line with the field, and that slow shift is a current. It dies away over minutes. A leakage current runs through the insulation and stays. The tester shows voltage ÷ current. So as the first two die away, the reading climbs. Water or dirt adds leakage, and leakage does not die away. It swamps the absorption, so the reading hardly climbs. Step from Dry to Wet.

pages.name: A ratio ignores the weather
pages.text: A single reading swings with temperature. As a rule of thumb, insulation resistance halves for every 10 °C rise and doubles for every 10 °C fall. So a reading on a warm day can look worse than last month's, with nothing wrong. PI and DAR take two readings close together, on the same cable, at the same temperature. Warmth pulls both down together, so the ratio barely moves. At 20 °C the core reads 24.1 GΩ at 1 minute. At 40 °C the same sound core reads 6.0 GΩ, a quarter as much. Both bars slide down together, and the gap between their ends stays the same. Its PI stays at 2.66 the whole way.
pages.alt: The dry core from the last screen. Assume it was read at 20 °C, where it reads 24.1 and 64.0 GΩ. The sketch assumes both readings fall alike. Each mark along the bottom is ten times the last. pages.name: Check
pages.task: Two cores of one cable both read 3.00 GΩ at 1 minute, well over the client's 1 GΩ. At 10 minutes, core X reads 3.20 GΩ and core Y reads 9.00 GΩ. Which core has a steady leakage, such as moisture?
pages.alt: X's reading hardly climbs. PI = 3.20 ÷ 3.00 = 1.07, questionable. Most of X's current is steady leakage, and leakage does not die away. Y climbs to a PI of 9.00 ÷ 3.00 = 3.00, okay, as its absorption current dies.
pages.html: X's reading hardly climbs. PI = 3.20 ÷ 3.00 = 1.07, questionable. Most of X's current is steady leakage, and leakage does not die away. Y climbs to a PI of 9.00 ÷ 3.00 = 3.00, okay, as its absorption current dies.

pages.name: After the test: discharge
pages.text:
When the test stops, the core is a charged capacitor. One core of String B has 0.528 µF. At 5 kV it holds Q = C × V = 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000 = 0.00264 C = 2.64 mC. Its energy is E = ½ × C × V² = 0.5 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000² = 6.60 J. Part of the charge has soaked into the insulation. It seeps back out after the core has been discharged, and can bring the voltage back.

Never improvise the order. Check the tester's display shows discharged. Then the discharge stick, then the hook stick, then the hand earth. Earth the core and the screen at both ends.

Keep it discharging and earthed for at least five times as long as the test voltage was on. After a 1-minute spot reading, that is at least 5 minutes. Some older guidance says four times. Use five. Then leave the earths on until the next test needs them.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: L3 at 5 kV reads 17.5 GΩ at 30 s, 23.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 60.0 GΩ at 10 minutes. These are practice values. L3's DAR is 23.00 ÷ 17.50 = 1.31, satisfactory. Its PI is 60.00 ÷ 23.00 = 2.61, okay. It held the voltage for 10 minutes and beats the client's 1 GΩ. So it passes.
pages.alt: DAR = R60 s ÷ R30 s = 23.00 ÷ 17.50 = 1.31. Satisfactory: 1.25 to 1.6. PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 60.00 ÷ 23.00 = 2.61. Okay: 2 to 4. The voltage held for the full 10 minutes, and 23.0 GΩ beats the client's 1 GΩ. L3 passes. A DAR is done in 1 minute, where a PI takes 10. That makes it the quick check. It comes out lower than the PI. Its two readings are only 30 s apart, so it sees less of the climb. Makers draw the bands in other places. Some call a PI of 2.0 or more good, and a DAR of 1.4 or more. On those bands, L3's PI counts as good, but its DAR of 1.31 falls short.
pages.html:
DAR = R60 s ÷ R30 s = 23.00 ÷ 17.50 = 1.31. Satisfactory: 1.25 to 1.6.

PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 60.00 ÷ 23.00 = 2.61. Okay: 2 to 4.

The voltage held for the full 10 minutes, and 23.0 GΩ beats the client's 1 GΩ. L3 passes.

A DAR is done in 1 minute, where a PI takes 10. That makes it the quick check. It comes out lower than the PI. Its two readings are only 30 s apart, so it sees less of the climb.

Makers draw the bands in other places. Some call a PI of 2.0 or more good, and a DAR of 1.4 or more. On those bands, L3's PI counts as good, but its DAR of 1.31 falls short. The client's test spec decides pass or fail.

One more caution. Some insulation shows very little absorption, so its reading barely climbs even when it is sound. So read each core's PI beside its sister cores. The core that stands apart is the one to question.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why a PI or DAR tells you more about a cable's insulation than a single IR reading.
pages.why: A model answer: A single IR reading swings with temperature. Insulation resistance roughly halves for every 10 °C rise. So a reading on a warm day can look worse with nothing wrong. PI and DAR compare two readings on the same cable, close together, at the same temperature. So the ratio barely moves. The ratio also shows how the current behaves. In dry, clean insulation the charging and absorption currents die away and leave a small leakage. So the reading climbs, and the ratio comes out well above 1. In wet or dirty insulation a high, steady leakage hides the absorption. So the curve stays flat, and the ratio sits near 1. A core can beat the client's figure on one reading and still show a flat curve. The ratio catches it.

pages.task: Another cable's core reads 8.0 GΩ at 1 minute and 9.6 GΩ at 10 minutes. Determine its PI.

Same method, new numbers. These are practice values. Give it to 2 places. A ratio has no unit.

PI = R10 ÷ R1 = 9.6 ÷ 8.0 = 1.20

1.20 sits in 1 to 2, questionable. Find out why before you submit it.
